Returning something online should take five minutes; in reality it takes a trip most people never find time for. ReturnLoop connects a ready package with a driver already passing by, so the errand disappears.
The package sat by the door until the window closed; friends had the same story — not "I don't want to return things" but "I meant to, and then I didn't."
Is the problem that people don't know where to return things, or that the trip never fits a real day and never feels safe to hand off?
8 semi-structured interviews, ages 24–65, plus competitive review of Uber Return a Package, DoorDash Package Pickup, USPS/UPS/FedEx/Amazon.
The return window is the real villain.
"If I need to print a label, I give up." — Alex
A failed drop-off trip kills momentum.
Trust came up more than price did.
Recruited to test whether the problem differs for a less app-fluent user; for younger participants the barrier was time, for her it was confidence.
Neither competitor is built around the sender's experience or offers proof beyond a photo. That's the gap.
"It just sits there. I'll do it tomorrow." (Jack)
Flexible pickup window, not instant dispatch
"If I need to print a label, I give up." (Alex)
Sender scans the digital label / barcode
"Who is this, and did it arrive?" (nearly everyone)
Live tracking and independent carrier confirmation
The Moment the Design Had to Change
v1 marked a return complete the instant a driver scanned it; two interview stories proved that wasn't enough, so the flow now waits for carrier confirmation.
Personas were grouped by why people stalled, not by demographics, so each represents a distinct reason the process breaks down.
Where emotional low points occur and what resolves them.
Driver chat gives a human channel (Margaret)

DoorDash built a return pickup feature in 2023 and none of the participants knew it existed. The problem wasn't a missing feature, it was a missing experience. Uber and DoorDash proved the mechanic works; what they didn't build is the trust.
People don't want a cheaper return — they want one they don't have to think about twice.
AI-powered planning app that scaffolds executive function until the student no longer needs it.

ASAP is an AI-powered mobile app designed to help college students build independent planning skills by breaking assignments into manageable steps scaffolding executive function until the student no longer needs the tool.
For many students planning was never taught. It was just expected.

When students move from high school to college, three external supports vanish at once: fixed schedules, adult intervention, and peer accountability. The system that managed their behavior was never designed to transfer ownership to them.
“In high school, 70% of the structure was externally provided. In college I have to do the exact opposite, and I don't know where to begin.”
Age when the prefrontal cortex fully matures
AI accelerated every phase. We directed every decision.
A map of the problem space in hours. Synthesized root causes of EF deficits.
The judgment to identify which 5 of 15 insights actually mattered for design.
Contextual empathy. Data synthesis lacks the nuance of student stress.
Ideas rendered before we'd fully articulated them. Interactive flows instantly.
The discipline to reject 83 versions and know why 84 was right.
Micro-interactions that build habit. It generates screens, not behaviors.
3 synthetic personas to run heuristic reviews before human testing.
Real human testing that uncovered the psychological weight of UI copy.
Emotional variability, mood-based decision-making. That required a real human.

The wireframe boards are in the file and they are strong — numbered, state by state, with the AI prompt copy already written in ("not sure where to start? I can help break this into steps"). Show them as boards, not as individual screens: each is a labelled row of three states.
Home, three states: empty · with task · completed
Note: The flow was tested across four distinct groups (student, career-changer, ECP, entrepreneur) with 16 boards total.
No overwhelming lists. The interface focuses the student entirely on the next immediate action.
AI suggests subtasks with reasons and estimates, student edits freely
The app breaks down complex assignments, providing estimates and rationale, but the student edits freely.
Locks everything except the current task to build momentum.
Keeps track of time spent directly on the active task.
Visual indicator of progress towards fully independent planning.
The success of this app is measured by the student needing it less over time.

Google Calendar, Notion, Todoist, Apple Reminders, Monday.com, and Focus To-Do all sit in that left cluster — different feature sets, same job: hold the list for you, forever. Trevor AI gets closer, coaching and auto-scheduling, but it never lets go of the wheel.
ASAP is the only one built to work its way out of a job. Every other product wins when you open it again tomorrow. ASAP wins when you don't need to.
One task in, one step out; AI escalates help: clarify → break down → coach only when needed.
Felt the "Low confidence" label reflected on her, not the AI.
The emotional gap: Synthetic users were logical and consistent. Real users aren't. Mood governs motivation, and AI follows logic.
The feature we built to help was the one that caused harm.
Clinical label to signal AI uncertainty. AI testing flagged no issues.
Natural language that owns AI limitation without reflecting on the user.
Priya read the label as a judgment of herself, not the AI. For a first-generation student battling imposter syndrome, it did harm. Transparency without empathy is just data.
Ethics surface late — unless you look early
The confidence label harm only surfaced in Phase 4. One checkpoint at the start isn't enough.
Over-reliance is the core paradox — and it's unresolved
We built an AI tool to fix AI dependency. The students who need it most have to open it at the exact moment they're avoiding work.
A human in Phase 2 would have caught the confidence label and mood-priority gaps weeks sooner.
Research synthesis in hours. A prototype in one evening. Synthetic personas that caught structural issues before any real user saw them.
Synthetic users were emotionally flat. Figma Make broke under complexity. AI rewards shallow iteration if you let it.
Design for the worst day. Mood & energy need to be first-class inputs not edge cases. Next version needs a low-friction "I can't right now" mode.
"The goal is not helping students finish work faster. It is helping them eventually not need the system at all."

Traveling with a pet shouldn't be a guessing game. Every country, airline, and document comes with different rules, deadlines, and requirements. PetClear gives you a personalized checklist based on your pet and travel route showing exactly what you need, where to get it, and when it's due. Everything organized. Everything tracked. No surprises at the airport.
Airlines take the pet fee and say nothing about what comes next. Owners arrive at the airport missing a document they never knew existed.
Requirements invisible during booking — NOC, fitness certs, timing windows.
Airline, vet, blog, forum all disagree on what is actually required.
Docs lost in camera rolls, every trip starts from scratch.

10 airline policy pages reviewed, r/pettravel and r/expats threads read, then every airline called directly. The same gap appeared every time — no route-specific, animal-specific document checklist anywhere.
Checklist only after booking — too late.
No timing windows or USDA endorsement.
No NOC mention anywhere on the page.
Verdict: Every airline listed carrier sizes and fees, none generated a route-specific checklist.
Verdict: 5 of 7 airlines could not or would not give complete requirements on call — Lufthansa explicitly refused, only United was clear, for domestic only.
"I did everything I was supposed to do. Nobody told me there was more."
Travel with pet, no last-minute surprises; one trusted source; confirmed ready before the airport.
Any age, any pet, domestic or international — always underprepared by the system.
Airline website incomplete or vague. Conflicting answers across sources.
Five real participants. Different failure points.
A standalone tool, not a feature inside an airline app. Enter pet and route, get exact documents, sources and lead times.
PetClear does not change any regulation. It makes existing requirements visible, organised, and timely — at the right moment.
Identifies breed, route checklist with lead times.
One entry, one profile: Sign-up and login converge fast.
The scan is the trigger: Everything upstream is setup, downstream is the live trip.
Branch to track, merge to remember: Destination and document tracking run parallel, then fold into shared history.

Pay pet fee, no requirements shown →
Missing docs flagged with sources and lead times
Arrive at airport → first time hearing about the document →
No surprises at the check-in counter.
Fewer denied boardings, fewer pets left behind.
Owners who avoided travel now have clarity to go ahead.
"The problem was never the rules. It was that nobody made them visible."
